findings.title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context and get cancelled when the request returns
findings.body:
Each background goroutine (Create here, and likewise Delete at 110, Update at 135 and DeleteCollection at 163) wraps the incoming request `ctx` with `context.WithTimeoutCause`. The apiserver/net/http cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after the goroutine is spawned.

As a result, the legacy SQL write will very often fail with `context canceled` before or while it runs. The 10s timeout never applies. The "safe measure" legacy copy silently goes stale, and the only trace is a metric, because the error is not logged.

Fix: use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent. That keeps request-scoped values such as identity and the logger, but drops the cancellation.

findings.title: Unordered fire-and-forget legacy writes can apply out of order and leave legacy inconsistent
findings.body:
Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy store, with no ordering, serialization or retry.

A create quickly followed by an update or delete of the same object (as the integration tests do) can reach legacy in any order. For example, the legacy Delete goroutine may run before the legacy Create goroutine. That leaves an orphaned row in legacy that is never cleaned up. An Update can likewise run before the Create and fail.

Since mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback for rolling back modes, this silently corrupts the fallback data. A per-object ordering mechanism, or at least logging and reconciliation, is needed.

findings.title: Legacy write errors are no longer logged
findings.body:
The previous implementation logged failures from the legacy store. In the new goroutines (Create here, and also Delete, Update and DeleteCollection), the legacy error is used only as a boolean for the duration metric and then discarded.

There is no log entry with the object name or kind or the error cause. Divergence between unified and legacy storage, including the context-cancellation failures, cannot be diagnosed. Log the error inside each goroutine.

findings.title: Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy metric
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage create failures are therefore reported as legacy failures, and the storage error metric never sees them. Dashboards and alerts on dual-writer health will be wrong.

findings.title: Storage Update failure is recorded as a legacy metric
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage update errors are therefore attributed to legacy storage in the metrics.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
findings.body: Inside the background goroutine, the legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection timings and failures are therefore counted as unified-storage observations, which skews both series.

findings.title: Object name used as the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)
findings.body:
The success path of Delete calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. It passes the resource `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

This mislabels the metric. Worse, it creates a new Prometheus time series for every distinct object name deleted, which is unbounded label cardinality and can blow up memory in Grafana and in the metrics backend. Use `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Delete stores the base logger in context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` attaches the base logger rather than the `log` built on the previous line, which carries the name, kind and method values. Every other method uses `log`. Logs emitted by downstream storage code during Delete lose the object name and method context.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object persisted in unified storage
findings.body:
The previous code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so legacy received exactly the object stored in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`.

That makes legacy compute its own result via `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)`. For patches, the patch is applied against the legacy copy, which may differ from storage. For PUTs, the object carries unified-storage resourceVersion and preconditions, which legacy may reject.

The two stores can therefore silently diverge, or legacy updates can fail. It also reuses a request-scoped objInfo after the request has completed. Restore the wrapper so legacy receives `res`.

findings.title: Delete no longer removes legacy copy when the object is missing in unified storage
findings.body:
The old implementation treated `NotFound` from unified storage as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. Now any storage error, including NotFound, returns early and skips the legacy delete.

Objects that exist only in legacy, such as ones never migrated or ones whose async create to unified storage was lost, can no longer be removed through the API. They remain as stale data in legacy.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests never verify the legacy write happens
findings.body:
Legacy and unified storage share one mock, and the legacy calls run in untracked goroutines that may execute after the test returns. None of the Mode3 tests assert that the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection was invoked, or with which arguments.

The core new behavior, asynchronous propagation to legacy, is untested. That is why bugs like the cancelled-context issue and the wrong metric calls go unnoticed.

The failure case also configures the error via `setupLegacyFn` even though it is named "unified store fails", so the test only passes because the mock is shared. Consider separate mocks and a synchronization point, for example `assert.Eventually` on `AssertCalled`.

findings.title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries
findings.body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which already exists on the line directly above it in the same hunk. It also pulls in unrelated older otel and plugin-sdk sums that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. This looks like accidental local tooling churn and should be reverted or regenerated cleanly.
